style_when: the story is a product, a device, a price or a market for a thing the reader could buy — an appliance, a panel, a router, a robot arm
prompt: Studio product photograph of a heavy anodized aluminum compute blade structurally partitioned by illuminated amber acrylic dividers, resting on a textured dark basalt studio surface. Shot with an 85mm studio telephoto lens at a razor-sharp focal plane, shallow depth of field. Asymmetric composition with the fractioned module off-centre on the thirds, leaving generous editorial negative space. Single softbox key light with visible falloff creating a long contact shadow across the stone. Crisp catalogue clarity, premium brushed metal textures, no gradient sweep.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, UI, printed text, plain gradient sweep
rationale: The studio object treatment isolates the compute module as a purchasable commodity, structurally divided by the new 'product'—the fractioning software layer—rendered as a premium physical object.
subject: a heavy compute blade partitioned by illuminated acrylic dividers
core_thesis: The software layer that fractions and schedules GPU compute has become the primary product differentiator as specialized chips overtake general-purpose GPUs.
core_conflict: Hardware commoditization vs software-defined compute fractioning
alt_text: The GPU Scheduling War. A heavy compute blade partitioned by illuminated amber acrylic dividers on a dark stone surface.
caption: The GPU Scheduling War: Why the fight for AI capacity moved off the single chip.
